written.myAnswer: Increasing substrate concentration increases the reaction rate until all enzyme active sites are occupied. Once the enzyme is saturated, adding more substrate does not increase the rate.
Pepsin works best in an acidic medium (about pH 2), while trypsin works best in an alkaline medium (about pH 8).
Optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate. Optimum pH is the pH at which it shows maximum activity.

As temperature rises toward the optimum, enzyme activity generally increases. At temperatures well above the optimum, heat disrupts bonds and the enzyme loses its globular structure and becomes denatured, causing its activity to decrease rapidly.

Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it is most active. A change in pH can alter the ionization of amino acids at the active site, reducing or stopping enzyme activity. For example, pepsin works in acidic conditions and trypsin in alkaline conditions.

Enzyme activity is affected by temperature, pH, and substrate concentration. Activity is greatest at the enzyme’s optimum temperature and pH; temperatures well above the optimum can denature the enzyme, and a pH change can reduce or stop activity. Increasing substrate concentration raises the reaction rate until all active sites are occupied, after which the rate levels off.
